lines: A one-line currency-rounding fix goes out, and a naive equality check between old and new output comes back with an enormous pile of rows reported as changed.
That report is technically true. It's also completely useless, because nobody can review a pile that size row by row.
A column-level summary of the exact same change says something very different: one column moved, by a known amount, and every other column stayed untouched.
Same underlying change. One report blocks review. The other one actually enables it.
Worth sitting with this before the reveal answers it directly.
A full join-diff compares old and new output column by column, and it genuinely is exact, missing nothing.
Does being exact mean a diff has to physically read every single row to get there?
Or is there a way to stay exact without reading everything?
steps.answer: No, exactness doesn't require reading every row. A checksum computed over an entire range of rows is itself an exact comparison -- if it matches on both sides, nothing in that range changed, and it never had to be read row by row at all.

lines: Here's the first of the two real strategies, the straightforward one.
Join the old output and the new output together on their shared key.
Compare every single column for every single joined row, side by side.
Exact and complete, yes -- but it reads every row on both sides, every time, whether anything in that row actually changed or not.
Here's the second strategy, built specifically to avoid that full read.
Take a range of keys and compute one checksum over that whole range, on both sides.
If the two checksums match, skip the entire range -- nothing in it changed, and none of it gets read row by row.
If they don't match, split that same range into smaller ranges and check each one the same way, recursing down until the actual differing rows are found.
steps.takeaway: A matching checksum proves a whole range is unchanged without reading it.

lines: One more question worth predicting before it gets answered for real.
Take the exact same underlying total, computed by summing the exact same pieces, just in a different order.
That can land on a measurably different floating-point value, not just in theory but in an actual run.
Does a diff that notices that difference have found a real regression worth reporting?
steps.answer: No, not automatically. Floating-point addition is not associative, so a harmless reordering inside a pipeline's own aggregation can shift the last few digits of a total with absolutely nothing having gone wrong.

lines: Here's that exact situation, run for real, side by side with an actual bug.
One harmless reordering, changing nothing real, and one genuine planted regression -- both go through the very same diff.
An exact, zero-tolerance comparison flags both of them as changed, with no way to tell them apart.
A tolerance band set around a defensible size lets the harmless reordering pass clean, while the real regression still gets caught, because it's simply too large to fit inside that same band.
Back to that same planted bug now, read a completely different way.
Rather than reporting a raw count of rows that differ, this summary names the single column where the real change actually lives.
It states how many rows that one column touched, and the size of the move in that column alone.
Every other column in the table gets reported as genuinely untouched, which a raw row count could never say on its own.
steps.takeaway: A usable diff report names the column, not just the row count.

lines: Now the cost of each strategy, measured directly rather than assumed.
Hold the actual number of real changes fixed, and grow the size of the table underneath them.
A full join-diff's cost grows right alongside the table, because it always reads the entire thing regardless of how much of it changed.
Checksum bisection's cost barely grows at all under the same conditions, so its advantage over the full join-diff keeps widening as the table gets bigger.
steps.takeaway: Bisection's advantage over a full join-diff grows with the table, not with the bug count.

lines: Pulling the two strategies and the two extra tools together now.
Both strategies are genuinely exact, and the choice between them is a cost tradeoff, not a correctness one.
A tolerance band separates harmless floating-point noise from an actual regression, so neither gets mistaken for the other.
And a column-level summary turns an unreviewable row count into a report a person could actually act on.
steps.takeaway: An exact diff can still choose how much of the table it actually has to read.

lines: One real run to close on, the same table and the same planted bug through both strategies at once.
Run the full join-diff against it, and separately run checksum bisection against the identical table and the identical bug.
Both strategies have to land on exactly the same set of changed rows for either one to be trustworthy at all.
Does the full join-diff end up reading roughly the same number of rows as checksum bisection, or does one of them read dramatically fewer?
steps.answer: Bisection reads dramatically fewer rows. Both strategies find exactly the same changed rows, but the full join-diff reads the entire table every time, while bisection only ever reads the specific ranges whose checksum actually came back mismatched.
